ELI5: How does a mirror reflect light?

ELI5 quantum electrodynamics? Sure why not it's midnight and I've had some wiskey. Light (being a wave) causes the electrons in your mirror to bounce back and forth at the same frequency as the light wave bounces back and forth. That cancels out the incoming wave, but it makes those same electrons emit an anti-wave (imagine the wave upside down), in the opposite direction. Mirrors can do this because they have a sheet of shiny metal in them, and shiny metals are shiny because their electrons are free to move around inside the material, which also gives those electrons the freedom to be bounced back and forth by incoming light waves and to emit anti-light waves of their own.

Want an interesting bit of trivia? The frequency of the light wave determines how easily it will be bounced by this method. Really big, long, slow waves like radio waves emitted from your cellphone don't really care what the electrons in a a lot of things are doing and pass right through walls and other stuff easily, or maybe it would be more accurate to say they go around. You can imagine it the same way you would imagine waves in water, when a wave becomes long enough or slow enough it is kind of like a tsunami, the wave just slowly fills the region from the bottom up ignoring all the little obstacles in the way. On the other hand, really small, fast, energetic waves like X-rays don't care for the opposite reason, and they pass right through your mirror like bullets piercing something too big and fluffy to really stop them. Visible light waves are just the right size to bounce off of mirrors and that's why we see reflections in our mirrors with our eyes, but if our eyes could see X-rays or gamma rays maybe some other type of material would appear reflective while mirrors appeared transparent.

Most materials bounce light off them. Really it's not that mirrors double light, so much as if you've just got a wall instead of a mirror, about half your light is hitting the wall and getting absorbed. (It'll very slightly make the wall warmer in the process.)

There's two things here, one is how much light is absorbed, and the other is how smooth it is. for example if you've got a really smoothly polished wooden table or countertop, (like this) you might be able to see the light reflecting off it if you're at the right angle. It still won't work as a mirror, even though it's smooth, because it absorbs too much light.

If you have a bit of scratched metal, it would bounce enough light off, but as it's scratched, it'd bounce off all over the place as it isn't smooth. See here.

If you smooth out that metal, and put it behind glass, then you have something that bounces all the light off, and bounces it all back in the correct direction because it's smooth. That'll work as a mirror.

This particular lifestyle-changing night I was heading home from a late night at work (I was a nurses aid at the time, just off the 3pm-11pm shift), when I stopped into that 24-hour temple of caloric delight, Walmart. I was a naive proto-hambeast myself, having never scaled back my diet as I passed into adulthood. It was my first shift back after vacation, so I was restocking 'essentials' (chips, dip, sugarwater, but there was milk and eggs too) at near-on midnight. Whenever I shop, whether its groceries or Home Depot, I try to guess what another customers' plans are; it's a little game I started back when I worked retail.
I got in line behind what I thought were two ordinary, everyday people. They fit into a category in my brain as 'fatter than me', and they seemed nice enough human beings. Being a curious sort, as I unloaded my cart I eyed their purchases to begin my game. The conveyor ahead of me was laden with a landfill of gastric excess. Several bags of fried chicken leftover from the deli that day which was probably taken from the discount cart, a literal bucket of potato salad, several bags of chips (the same brand as the ones in my cart, no less), several bottles of ranch dressing, a few bottles of soda, a few boxes of ice cream sandwiches. "Ahah!", I said to myself, naively. "These fine people must assuredly be preparing for a big family reunion picnic tomorrow!"
And it was in that instant that one of the people purchasing these items turned to the other and uttered a sentence that I will remember till the day I die, a sentence which keeps me on the treadmill an extra mile, an utterance which haunts me whenever I pass a McDonalds, a corpulent mewling which gnaws my soul whenever I get offered a refill on my drink. "Oh my gawd, I can't wait to get home so we can eat all this."
Its mate (I could barely tell their genders as both had unkempt hair as greasy as their sparsely stubbled collection of chins), turned to the speaker and responded, "I know! I'm soooo hungry! It's a good thing this place never closes, huh?" And then they embraced or at least attempted to, their bellies hanging out of their t-shirts over the overstressed waistbands of their sweatpants, their flabby arms failing to fit around each other. My eyes had opened as it grappled with what I was witnessing. At midnight, in the middle of the work week, it was possible for people to go out into the night and purchase enough foodstuffs to feed several dozen people, and apparently consume it all before dawn. I was still stunned as they loaded their shopping cart and waddled off into the night and the tired woman behind the register muttered her standard pleasantry started to ring up my own groceries.
I came to my senses as she scanned the milk and asked if I wanted it bagged. I started grabbing things off the conveyor and putting them back into the cart, stating that I just realized I couldn't afford anything but the milk and eggs. I had money to pay for it all, but I couldn't afford diabetic supplies, I couldn't afford XXXL sweatpants, I couldn't afford to let myself go down that adipose-choked path. As I paid for the only two healthy things in my cart, the register lady shook her head with a smile and said, "Good for you, sonny."
I had my first annual physical in years after that; and found out that not only was I diabetic but that my cholesterol levels were actually unreadable due to the sheer amount of fat floating around in my blood. My doctor told me it was a miracle I'd avoided a serious cardiac incident. In the two years since, thanks to cooking my own meals and plenty of daily exercise I've finally gotten off of insulin, my good cholesterol is high and my bad cholesterol is low, and for the first time my triglycerides were in the double digits. My struggle is not finished; I still take a low dose of metformin to maintain blood sugar and I'm on one of the weaker cholesterol medications. It hasn't been easy, but I've seen easy and I can't let easy happen to me.
Alright, gather around y'all. Lemme tell you about how late-night grocery shopping saved my life.
